Public Works-Quebec-harbours and rivers -Ellis bay, harbour improvements, $300,000.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
On the last occasion
the committee had under consideration the item, "Ellis bay, harbour improvements, $300,000". Shall the item cany?
Has the minister any information to give in regard to this item?

speakeroldname: Hon. J. C. ELLIOTT (Minister of Public Works):
speechtext:
Perhaps I shall give some information on this item if my hon. friend requests it. The report of the engineer shows that Ellis bay, formerly called Gamache bay, is situated near the southwest end of Anticosti island at a distance of 345 miles below Quebec. The island has an area of 31,000 square miles. All timber land is the property of a syndicate, the Anticosti Corporation, which is now de-

veloping the island for the purpose of settling it and for the production of pulpwood, which will be manufactured into pulp and paper at the following mills: the St. Maurice Valley Corporation, Three Rivers, Quebec; Port Alfred Pulp and Paper Corporation, Port Alfred; Wayagamack Pulp and Paper Company, Limited, Three Rivers. Port Menier on Ellis bay has been selected as the community and store centre where the town is being built, it being also the most protected place for the establishment of a harbour. The Anticosti Corporation has under way at the present time a scheme for the development of this harbour, which involves the expenditure of approximately $2,500,000 exclusive of railroads, dwellings and buildings which it will be necessary to construct on the island. Construction work was commenced by the company on December 1, 1926 and two ships berths were ready on June 1, 1927, a new commercial wharf on July 31 last, and harbour works completely finished by December 1, 1927. The report of the engineer is that this development scheme will be of great aid to shipping in the gulf of St. Lawrence, as it is proposed to make Ellis bay the provisioning centre for ships in the gulf where coal and fresh water will be obtainable at the new aommercial wharf. There will also be adequate protection for shipping in time of bad weather and a sea-going tug will be kept on hand to render assistance to ships in distress in the gulf. District Engineer Sabourin reporting on March 23, 1927-that was before the vote came before the house-estimated that outgoing there were 1,000,000 tons of pulpwood, valued at $5,000,000, and 3,000 persons; and incoming 3,000 persons, 400 horses and 55,500 tons of fuel and machinery estimated at $2,000,000. The population at the present time is 3,000 which it is expected will greatly increase in the near future. I find that a few years ago the island of Anticosti, which is a Canadian island, formerly owned by Mr. Menier, who is not a Canadian, was used largely for pleasure purposes, although there were about 1,200 acres farmed. The report of the farming operations is that there were raised oats, 'wheat, barley and various garden vegetables. The island is reported to be suitable for farming purposes after the timber is taken off. The company propose to ship pulpwood to their own mills, the Wayagamack, the St. Maurice and the Port Alfred, situated at different places in Canada, where the pulp will be manufactured into paper in our own Canadian mills. A few years ago the population was from 250 to 400; already that has increased to over 3,000, and it is expected that before midsummer it will be over 5,000.

Supply-Harbours and Rivers-Quebec
The estimate of the company is that there are 15,000,000 cords of pulpwood on the island; they were to ship 300,000 cords last year, the same amount this year and 420,000 cords in subsequent years, to these three paper companies. It is estimated that the re-growth each year will amount to 450,000 cords, so there will be a margin of 30,000 cords after taking off the 420,000 cords each year, which should provide for the continuation of this business for many years to come. That is the best information I am able to obtain on the subject. I understand the people working there are being well paid, and this is a reliable corporation. I had not looked up the matter for almost a year, and the other day I was under the impression that this was an American concern, but that is not so. It is practically an all-Canadian company, and it is expected that the 420,000 cords of pulpwood taken off annually, valued at about $5,000,000, will be manufactured into $25,000,000 worth of paper in Canada each year for many years to come. Then there is the additional consideration that this is very close to the main channel of the St. Lawrence and is recommended by the engineer as the best port of shelter in that district.
I would like to ask the minister if this company holds the island in freehold or whether it merely has timber rights?
They bought it out absolutely.

Then this town which
is being built will be what is termed a company town?

Yes, it will be largely a
company town; the company will own the land and I believe they are giving their employees the houses. I understand a large number of houses have been constructed and more are in process of construction.

The minister has said that
he expects the population to reach 3,000 instead of the 250 to 400 people now there. Are these additional people to be immigrants or are they to be Canadians?

I understand that is the
number there now, and they are nearly all Canadians.
Are they immigrants?

No, I am told they are
nearly all Canadians.
Then this is merely shifting the population from one section of Canada to another.

After the explanation of this matter made by the hon. member for Quebec South, it is quite apparent to me that this vote is for a commercial company which is on the island with the express purpose of taking off all the pulpwood they can and then leaving the island. This is not an immigration scheme in any sense, and I do not know why this very rich company should not be able to dredge their own channel. Neither do I know why the idea of a shelter should be brought in now for the first time.
I think this vote should be cut down considerably ; in fact, I have a motion here that the vote of $300,000 be reduced by $290,000. I do not think this sort of thing should go on; we should not assist a private company of this kind when there are so many other things in Canada urgently needed.

Here I believe we are face
to face with one of the most deplorable features of Canadian development. After all the minister has said, apparently this is a foreign company which possesses this island as freehold property, and which has no further interest in it than to denude it of all its trees. When that is done it will be of no use either as a fishing centre or as a shelter, develop it as we may. I think before this vote is carried some assurance should be given that timber of a certain size will be preserved, and that sufficient timber will be kept growing to preserve the settlement which is already there and to leave the island in a habitable condition. In too many places in Canada the pulpwood companies are simply taking off all the trees and leaving the land fit for no other use. I think some assurance should be given that, timber will be preserved on this island for all time to come.

I have in my hand the [DOT]prospectus of the Anticosti Corporation, issued at the time the bonds were issued. It would appear that this corporation paid the Menier family $6,000,000 for the island, thereby obtaining all the rights to the hunting, fishing, farming and forestry previously held by the Menier family. As the minister has said, this corporation is composed of the Wayaga-maek Rilip and Paper Company, the St. Maurice Valley Corporation, and- the Port Alfred Pulp and Paper Corporation, the last two being Sir Herbert Holt companies and the first ian independent concern. As soon as they acquired ownership of this island

Supply-Harbours and Rivers-Quebec
they issued bonds to the exitenit of $6,000,000; that is to say, they asked the public to subscribe $6,000,000, to enable .them to pay for this island. All the common! shares of tihe corporation are owned by these three companies, so with the public's money they purchased the property and now they want the public, that is to say parliament as representing itihe public of Canada, to make them a gift of some $500,000 more to help pay the interest on the bonds; already issued. That is practically the situation from the financial standpoint.
With regard to the expenditure by this company at Ellis bay or dsewhere, I find .in the prospectus that twenty^eight miles of railway have been built already, aparently out of the $2,500,000 mentioned by the minister.
No, that is not true.
Does the minister mean, to tell me that over and above this $6,000,000 the Anticosti Corporation paid for a railway? If that were the case I would 'be very much surprised.
My information is that they are spending $2,500,000 exclusive of railways, and dwellings-this is the report from the engineer-and other buildings, which will be necessary to construct on the island.

I do not know whether they spent money on the harbour. There was already in existence one harbour with sheltered deep water at the time the property was purchased. If they are finding it necessary to build two more I do not see why the government should be called upon to help pay for them.
We have too many of these large corporations in Quebec-I am not opposing corporations because they are large, nor wealthy men because they are wealthy-who are constantly coming to the federal, provincial and municipal governments, asking for assistance; when people of lesser means are unable to obtain assistance. This Anticosti Corporation is possibly one of the wealthiest in Canada. It is not undertaking development or colonization -work, and in saying that I am Sorry to have to contradict the minister. Those who know anything about the lumber and pulpwood business in the part of the country from which I come know that it is the intention of this company simply to go on the island, cut off the pulpwood and then move away. I do not think anyone Who has any knowledge of the pulp and paper situation, or the pulp and paper people in Quebec, will deny that statement. It is said that there are 15,000,000 cords of pulpwood on the island,
fMr. Power.]
but I doubt that very much. As a matter of fact, when this purchase was' made, the people who knew simply smiled and said, "Ain't it costly?", and they called it the ain't-it-costly corporation. It was not costly to the companies themselves, because the public subscribed to the bonds and if there is any profit it will go to the common stock, which helps the companies.
I do not believe there is any intention of remaining there in perpetuity. No pulp mills are being erected there, but only wharves and railways to take the pulpwood from the forest, put it on the vessels, and transport it to Port Alfred and Three Rivers. The prospectus says that the total cut will be 420,000 cords. If they cut that much they are cutting far more than the annual growth. As I said before, there is not 15,000,000 cords, and in the second place, the annual growth would not be more than two per cent under very favourable circumstances. Under the conditions that obtain here the trees do not grow fast, and the annual growth would hardly be one-half of one per cent, so there is no possibility of this being a permanent settlement, or of people remaining there after the island has been cut over.
I would suggest to the minister that instead of pressing for this item he leave it over for another year and see whether or not the statements which I have made are true. If it can 'be shown to me that there is any question of colonization here, or a permanent settlement, I have no objection to any development being carried on. I am told that the amount for dredging this summer will be $200,000, and that all of last yeans' vote has not been expended. We could Pot spend possibly more than $200,000 or $250,000 this year, and I u'ould ask the minister to reduce his estimate and if it is found at the next session of the house that there is really something worthwhile encouraging here, then we could vote more money.
Would you agree to the reduction I suggested?
What was that?
I proposed to reduce that by $290,000, making the amount $10,000.

If there is any real dredging to go on with, and if the dredges are there. I would suggest t'halt possibly there be $100,000 or $150,000 expended this year. By next year we would know whether there was any real reason for it.

I do not want to prolong the debate or the session, because I know

Supply-Harbours and Rivers-Quebec
everybody is anxious to get away, but I cannot let this matter pass without saying a few words, particularly in view of the fact that this item has reference to a place which is situated in the county which I have the honour to represent in this house.
At the outset of my remarks I may state to my hon. friend from Quebec South (Mr. Power) that I am very much surprised at the stand he is taking to-day. When there was a vote before the house that had to do with some appropriation for the province, when we were called upon to vote an item of $8,500,000 for the harbour of Quebec, at the head of which his brother presides, he did not object. I think it ill behooves the hon. gentleman to quarrel with other sections of the province and other parts of the community where necessary improvements must be made just as much as in the district of Quebec, and which in the future may be much more beneficial to the country than even those which are being carried on in the district he represents.
The question has been raised by the hon. member for Rosetown (Mr. Evans) and the hon. member for Quebec South as to whether Anticosti island would ever be colonized, and if there would be any farming earned on in that thriving community. I have a book here entitled Le Canada et 1'Emigration Francaise, by Mr. Frederic Geirbie.
In 1881, long previous to the acquisition of the island by Mr. Menier, the French senator, colonization was going on. There were settlements and farms at that time. The reason these people ceased their operations was that when Mr. Menier took possession of the island he made it a sort of national park or summer resort. He filled the rivers and lakes with fish and used the island only for his own purposes for a few weeks in the spring, summer and fall. In 1881 there were 102 occupants, and 106 proprietors; there were 89S acres of occupied land, and 427 acres of improved land and pasture, including gardens and orchards. The crops at that time, in 1881, were 51 bushels of oats, 133 bushels of barley, 11,610 bushels of potatoes, 1,178 bushels of turnips and 58 tons of hay. Progress was being made steadily at the time Mr. Menier took possession of the island. When he did take possession he had certain lands improved, and conducted some farming operations himself, as is shown by the census of 1921. If hon. gentlemen would look at page 399 of the Census of Canada. 1921, they would see that Anticosti island had 1,246 acres of pasture, 196 acres of cereals and flax. There were further farm operations conducted at that time, as follows: 21 acres
of forage crops, 24 acres of potatoes and roots, 100 acres cultivated, for barley, producing 1,400 bushels, and 80 acres sown to oats producing 350 bushels. This was the development in the little village Mr. Menier had there, wherein was situated the church, the convent, the butcher shop, the grocery shop, the police station, the fire department, and the farm which he owned.
These things had been accomplished by Mr. Menier himself, and everything was turned over to the Anticosti Corporation for the sum of $6,000,000. This amount was paid in ready cash by the three companies mentioned by the Minister of Public Works, namely, the Wayagamack-Pulp and Paper Company, the St. Maurice Valley Corporation, and the Port Alfred Paper Company, which are three of the largest pulp and paper companies in Quebec and perhaps in Canada. These companies have bought the island for $6,000,000. According to the figures which I have under my hand the corporation have spent $1,500.000 in starting the construction of two wharves in addition to the wharf that was built in the early days by Mr. Menier. These two new large wharves have been constructed in order to enable big vessels to come in and load cargoes of pulpwood for the three companies whose names I have mentioned. In addition to that the corporation have built houses for their men and an hotel for the people coining there. The expenditure on this work up to the present time is nearly $2,000,000. That has been done during the eighteen months that the new corporation has been in possession of the island.
If I remember well, when I was there in 192b and 1926, at the time of the two last general elections, only Mr. Menier and those associated with his business were on the island, but in August, 1926, this corporation came into being and since then the island has been a beehive of industry, many people having found their way there and have been enabled to earn their bread and butter in that part of the province of Quebec. Had it not been for this undertaking many of them would have been turned away from Quebec and Canada and w'ould have had to go to the United States. As the Minister of Public Works has said, there are on the island at present three thousand Canadian-born or naturalized Canadian subjects who are earning their living and receiving salaries running from at least $75 a month to as much as $15,000 a year, that being the salary which the general manager, Mr. J. H. Valiquette, is paid for the work of running the whole business of the Anticosti Corporation and developing the island.

As regards the question of colonization I have under my hand a letter from Mr. Francois Faure, General Manager of the company who is in charge of the operations of the whole island. He writes:
The first work done by the Anticosti Corporation was to make the necessary organization to exploit the forestry resources of the island, and the next step is the classification of the soil with a view to colonizing the island with good Canadians and immigrants.
A certain amount of this work had been done before Mr. Menier became the owner of the island and according to the company's letter, the original of which has been placed in the hands of the Minister of Public Works, it is their intention to do colonizing work later on when their activities in the pulpwood and lumber business have provided a sufficient area of cleared land to establish new settlements at different points. There was a miniature railway on the island when Mr. Menier was owner. Since that time larger railways have been built and in the very near future they will circle the island in order that the company may carry on their activities and accomplish the purpose for which they bought the island.

Can the hon. member
assure the committee that any person can go on the island without the permission of the company, and without being an employee of the company?

Persons who want to go on the island must be connected with the company, or have special business with the company, or have permission of the company to go there. There is nothing unusual about the island. There are, I am told, in Ontario and other provinces, certain territories where larger corporations conduct activities similar to those conducted by this company, where they are owners and proprietors of the land and where they have the right to order out people whom they do not want to be on their property. They are proprietors and owners of the whole area of the land, the Iroquois Falls, for instance, where the Abitibi Pulp and Paper Company is established.
Does the hon. member know of any case of that description in Ontario where public funds are being spent for the benefit of a company alone?

I do not know what
the practice is in Ontario or what is being done in the other provinces, but I know that last year when the Minister of Public Works was faced with a request similar to this one he inquired and found out what the proper procedure was and in what way these companies should be assisted if they were bona

fide corporations that really wanted to do something to develop the country. They started on a plan similar to the one carried on, I am told, in the United States. The government helps companies that have certain financial backing and when it is sure that they really intend to do something to develop the natural resources of the country. The same thing has been done in other provinces and I think we in Quebec are asking no more than has been asked and done in other provinces.
As regards the number of cords of pulp-wood that might be taken out of the island, before these people purchased the property an estimate was made of what they could get out of it in the way of timber. Mr. Piche, who I am told is one of the best authorities on the lumber industry not only in Quebec but in Canada and who it at the head of the forestry resources of the Quebec government, surveyed the whole island, and he gave his opinion that a minimum of 15,000,000 cords of pulpw'ood could be taken out of the island. Any person can estimate from the re-growth that will come later, there will still be on the island timber to be cut for pulpwood when nearly all the members of the present parliament have passed away.
As the Minister of Public Works has said, the wood is manufactured into paper in Canada, not a stick is being exported to the United States. This means that Canada reaps the full economic benefit of the whole territory. The management of the island of Anticosti is in the hands of a staff who are all Canadian citizens. Salaries and wages paid to labourers and others for the manufacture of pulpwood and other work in which the company was engaged during the operating season of 1927-28 amounted to about 82,000,000, and the raw material which is shipped to the different cities is manufactured there into paper which, as a finished product, is exported to the United States, or used in Canada when it is required by other paper mills in this country. This brings to Canada a revenue of approximately $12,000,000 per annum and this is the case when operations are not being carried1 on to full capacity because certain works have just been started.
What is the government asked to do? The government is asked only to dredge out a certain part of the channel so that it will be possible for .the boats of the company to come with safety to the two new wharves that have been constructed by the company. The government is not asked to dredge a harbour for the sole benefit of the company. It is asked only to dredge 'a channel from the main

Supply-Harbours and Rivers-Quebec
channel where the vessels come near the island to their wharves so that these vessels may come in to them with safety to load pnlpwood and -other products of the island. When I went there in 1925 and 1926 on the boat of the Clarke Steamship Company we had to remain about a mile and' a half or two miles upstream and we had to be taken by gasoline launches to the wharf of the Menier family, because there was no channel by which we could reach the wharf in safety. The government and the country owe it to the company, which has invested $6,000,000 of its own money in the island, which has spent more than $2,000,000 this year, and which will spend more than $2,000,000 in salaries and wages every year if it wants to develop the natural resources of the island, to give it an opportunity to have a proper channel from the main channel in the river St. Lawrence in order that boats may reach the wharves with safety.
During the 1928 season of navigation ten boats per week carrying mechandise, coal, cattle, horses, pulpwood and passengers will pass through this port. The number of passengers it is estimated will approximate from five (o ten thusand people going to and from the island. There are in addition the boats of the Clarke Steamship Company, which, under the terms of the subsidy given by this government, have to ply every week to these wharves. When there were hardly three or four hundred people on the island when it was owned by Mr. Menier, the vessel could anchor upstream, and that was sufficient for the small population of the island at that time, but now that the population has reached three thousand, and is likely to increase later on, it is necessary to provide facilities for the vessels of the Clarke Steamship Company and also for such vessels as will carry pulp and other products from the island, and as the Postmaster General reminds me, it will also enable the boats to carry the mails in safety.
This company has four vessels, one of which was recently built at a cost of many thousands of dollars: the George McKee, the Fleurus and the Savoy. The last two vessels were owned formerly by the Menier family. There is also the Sable "I", which is owned and operated by the Bras d'Or Navigation Company, but in which this company at Anticosti is interested, and which plies regularly from the spring right up until the fall, and even in the winter months, to that port and to the ports of Quebec and Montreal, with supplies of goods and passengers. The Postmaster General again reminds me that I have omitted to mention the revenue; he never forgets anything. In 1925-26 the revenue from the
port Menier post office was $319.23; in 1926-27, 86S5.06; in 1927-28, $2,285.31; so the revenue is increasing year by year and has greatly increased over what it was in 1925.
Formerly, when Mr. Menier used to occupy the island, apparently it was his own private property and practically no customs and excise duties were collected; they amounted to $57.97 in 1925-26; $37.63 in 1926-27, and in 1927-28, $585.19 was collected and accrued to the national revenue, so there is business being done in a regular way at that place, and I think that this is a proposition that is worthy of consideration and encouragement by all the members of the house.
I have no particular interest in this proposition myself. I do not own a cent of stock or of bonds of the company. I have never had any dealings with the company. I have never been on the island since this company was operating. I was there in 1925 and 1926 when the Menier family were owners of the island. When a company such as this is ready to undertake a large work of this kind in developing the natural resources of this country, I think we ought to give it the fullest possible assistance, and make it easier for the company to go on with its business.

Do I understand from
what the minister said that within a few years the revenue derived from the sales tax that will be paid on the sales of pulpwood or paper manufactured in Anticosti island will be sufficient to repay in full the amount that it is now proposed to expend on this work?

I cannot say just what
the exact revenue will be, but I am told by the Finance department that the business of all such companies helps the general business of the country. There will be a sales tax on the paper when it is manufactured, and there will also be income tax. Work of this kind all contributes to the general business of the country, and the more business there is, the more revenue the Finance department gets. The revenue from $25,000,000 worth of paper manufactured in Canada will be a very important revenue. The collection of the tax on the profits of the corporation will also bring in a considerable revenue to the treasury of Canada. The business that this company will carry on will materially aid the financial situation in this country.
I want to say to my hon. friend who asked the question with regard to whether anybody else is getting similar assistance, that this is a principle that has been followed for over twenty years; that is, where a company or an individual was coming in and starting a concern which would employ labour and pro-

Supply-Harbours and Rivers-Quebec
duee materials, tending to the general development of the country, the policy of the government has always been to help them by way of dredging, wharves, breakwaters and all that sort of thing. We are doing it for the Thunder Bay Pulp and Paper Company at Port Arthur. We are doing it for the United Grain Growers; we dredged a slip to their elevator at Port Arthur. We are doing it for the Saskatchewan Co-operative Grain Growers; we dredged a slip to their company elevator at Port Arthur. We did dredging for the elevator that was built in Sarnia. We are doing it for the Powell River Lumber Company in British Columbia. We are doing it similarly for coal companies. There is no difference in principle.

Are not all
these public ports, not private ports?

They are public ports,
but my hon. friend does not get the point. The dredging we did was dredging to enable them to get from the main stream to their elevators. That is just what is being done here, only in this case there is an additional advantage. I want to say to my hon. friend, because I know he wants to be fair, when he refers to the fact that there was no reference the other day to the fact that this was a harbour of shelter, what I read to him to-day were the details prepared over a year ago when this matter was submitted to the house, and when the house committed itself to the project, and the contract was let.
Somebody asked how much dredging was done. There was $187,000 of dredging done last year. I want to explain to the house that if they do not approve of this sort of thing, it is going to affect all similar projects. It includes, for instance, the coking plant at Hamilton; it includes the Manicouagan Company, Trinity bay and various other works.

But in these other cases
the companies do not own the whole town; they are not company towns.

They own the property
to which the slip is being dredged, but in this case, it is very near the main channel of the St. Lawrence. The engineers report that it is the most suitable place for a harbour of refuge in that part of the river. I do think that the dredging should proceed this year, and that it should proceed to the full amount of the item mentioned here. If I thought it were possible for us to do with less money, there is nobody more anxious than I am that we should get along with the least possible
[Mr. Elliott.)
amount, but this house committed itself, without any objection, to this work a year ago. I want the house to have all the information possible. I appreciate the discussion, because if this is the feeling of the house, then I want to know it.
Mr. ADSHEAD; The hon. gentleman made a statement a short while ago that nobody could go on the island without the consent of the company; that it was a company town and that the company owned all the stores.

Practically all the large
concerns keep control of their own property. Where a company is carrying on business operations, it is absolutely necessary that the public should not wander about at will over Ihe company's property. I think everybody will agree with that proposition. Take the steel companies, or the plant at Hamilton; take the Thunder Bay Pulp and Paper Company; take any of these works we are assisting, and the same rule applies.
Mr. BOYS; Are there not public highways through all the properties you are referring to?
I would not say so. I think the principle followed is exactly similar.
It seems to me the only justification is that possibly they would have no right to do dredging themselves. As I understand, the whole island is privately owned, and always has been. Am I right?
Quite so.

Then I take it for granted there has never been a survey resulting in highways which would be vested in the crown. The whole island is privately owned. That would not give the company the right to go out in navigable water and do work which is essential to the undertaking. It seems to me the vote must be justified on that ground. I do not think the minister would go so far as to suggest, that where an enterprise is privately owned, and the public have no right of access to any portion of the territory, it is the duty of the country to provide money for dredging. Another feature occurs to me in regard to the financing. I heard the hon. member for Quebec South (Mr. Power) intimate that tends to the extent of $6,000,000 had been offered to the public. I gathered that, the public had subscribed for them, and that the promoters would get the common stock for practically nothing. The minister has pointed out that this was undertaken last year, and it is important to know whether those who subscribed for the bonds did sc

in tihe expectation that the dredging would be proceeded with. That is certainly a very important feature, because, if so, it might be considered a breach of faith if the work were not carried out. Personally I should like to be enlightened on those points.

I am not in a position to say whether any bonds of the company were sold on the statement that the government had made any promise to do dredging. Certainly no bonds could have been so sold except after the item was passed by this house a year ago. I may tell my hon. friend that the government did not decide upon this policy without considering it very carefully and ascertaining the merits. I was led to believe, after a very careful investigation, that this was one of the best investments by way of dredging as a public work that the department could do. I believed it was a bona fide concern and would give employment to 5.000 people at good wages for many years to come. That is only the smaller part of the business, because I felt the company would supply the raw material to be manufactured 'to the highest possible extent within Canada, thus employing a great deal of labour.
Is not the labour absolutely in the 'hands of the company? In an ordinary community if a man loses his job he can get some other work in the locality; here he would have to get off the island.

My hon. friend misunderstands me. The pulpwood will be consumed in the paper mills at Port Alfred, St. Maurice and Three Rivers. It furnishes employment to the men on the boats engaged in moving the material and the men in the mills. Here is the situation: Instead of having the island of Anticosti absolutely unproductive, we now have a thriving population there, well provided for and receiving good wages'.
Is it not a fact that the men must spend their wages in the company's stores at the company's own prices?
I think it is. Last year 55,000 'tons of food products were brought in.
And sold by the company?
I have no doubt. However, Mr. Chairman, perhaps we can obtain sufficient information to satisfy everybody, and I am quite willing to suggest that the matter stand for further consideration.

One other question.
The minister has attempted to bolster up
his argument for the expenditure of the money by stating that it would make a good harbour of refuge for vessels. Remembering that this is private property, is there any agreement with the company to permit vessels to use the harbour in case of distress?

My information is that
they have always had that right.
It is in the gulf.

There are two St. Lawrence routes, one north of Anticosti and the other south. If my hon. friend will look at Port Ellis on the map he will find that this harbour is only a little off the direct route. Some 3,000 feet of dredging has to be done to get to the dock, but that is partially along the main channel. This is what the engineer reported a year ago when the matter was under consideration:
This development scheme will be a great aid to shipping in the gulf of St. Lawrence as it is proposed to make Ellis bay a provisioning centre for ships in the gulf where coal and fresh water will be obtainable at the new commercial wharf. There will also be adequate protection for shipping in time of bad weather and a seagoing tug will be kept on hand to render assistance to ships in distress in the gulf.

The minister's remarks
are very interesting. I listened also to the eloquent speech of my learned friend from Charlevoix-Saguenay (Mr. Casgrain), but I was very much surprised to hear him complain that the item for $8,500,000 for the harbour of Quebec had been voted.

I did not say that. I
said I was surprised to find there was not very much discussion of it at the time from the hon. member for Quebec South who is fighting this item now. Let us be fair with everybody.

Those two things are entirely different. The item for Quebec harbour is altogether different from the item for Ellis bay dredging. Now we are on the latter item. Because my hon. friend from Quebec South (Mr. Power) represents an important section of Quebec city-which is also represented by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe), the hon. member for Quebec West (Air. Parent) and the hon. member for Quebec-Montmorency (Air. Lavigueur)- and because money has been voted for the city of Quebec-and the fact of the matter is, it is not for the city of Quebec alone, but for the country at large-is no reason why any hon. gentleman should get up and suggest that the hon. member for Quebec South must necessarily remain silent in respect of any
3358	COMMONS
Supply-Harbours and Rivers-Quebec
vote for any other constituency. To say that because this house has voted $8,500,000 for Quebec, therefore the hon. member for Quebec South must necessarily keep his mouth shut when other items are under discussion, is no argument at all. When the item for Quebec was under consideration the hon. member for Charlevoix-Saguenay supported it; he voted for it. The hon. gentleman reminds me of that old maxim: Nemo allegans suam turpitudinem audiendus est-no one is allowed to allege his own turpitude.
The hon. member for Charlevoix-Saguenay should be glad to admit that light comes from discussion. The very interesting speech from the hon. member for Quebec South brought forth some illuminating explanations from the Minister of Public Works. Every hbn. member is free to speak in this house as he sees fit, and because a certain item has been voted for his constituency that is no reason why anyone should say he has not the right to express his own views regarding the advisability or otherwise of some other item. I crave the indulgence of this house to defend the rights of any member; any member has the right to say what he thinks about any item before the house. Because I get an item of $5,000 or $10,000 or more in my constituency, why should I shut my eyes to everything else that goes on here? Because a member gets so much for his constituency is he to be blind to what is going on somewhere else? One should be more independent than that, and I am sure that if my hon. friend from Charlevoix-Saguenay will think it over he will agree with me, and that when he speaks afterwards he will congratulate the hon. member for Quebec South on his freedom of speech.
I am not acting as lawyer in behalf of the hon. member for Quebec South; he can defend himself. But I would point out that the hon. member for Quebec South has nothing to do with the spending of the money voted for Quebec harbour; he has no more to do with it than has the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) or the hon. member for Quebec West (Mr. Parent). It is true his brother is chairman of the Quebec harbour commission, but he does well; and the best evidence that he does well is the fact that he remains in office. But these two gentlemen are separate individuals, and I admire the hon. member for Quebec South for being so independent. I do not believe the hon. member for Charlevoix-Saguenay has any ground for complaint against the chairman of the Quebec harbour commission. If so he should state

the fact. But whether he has any complaint or none in that regard why should he reproach the hon. member for Quebec South? This is something altogether different. The question he raised in the opening of his speech was more like the first course of a meal-hors d'oeuvres; it was really beside the question.
I am not particularly opposed to the vote, Mr. Chairman, but before we leave it I have two remarks to offer. The first is this. The population, we are told, has increased from 451 in 1921 to 3,000 at the present time-and 5.000 in midsummer. Well, I see the time when Anticosti island will be so thickly, so densely populated that it will be represented in the house by 'a distinct member. I do not know whether at that time the hon. member for Charlevoix-Saguenay will choose to represent Anticosti island or will devote his attention to Charlevoix-Saguenay. But there are a good many constituencies with a population of from 50,000 to 60,000; in my own constituency there are more than 50,000 people; and I wonder whether I should get ten times as much for my constituency- $3,000,000-because there is ten times the population there that Anticosti has during the summer. There is another thing, too. If any hon. member wishes to go to Anticosti island to get some idea of the improvements that will be carried on there next summer he will be barred. This is private property; you are not allowed to go there: "Keep off the grass; no trespassing 'allowed." But it is very strange. There is a sort of wall-
A wall of Jericho.

No, not a wall of Jericho,
because that wall fell down. But there is a wall around the island and no one can get in. I say, it is entirely private property, and there is room only for public expenditure. It is very strange, I repeat. But in Quebec city anyone can walk about on the streets; it is public. It is interesting to note the difference between the two places. No one can step on to Anticosti island because it is absolutely private, whereas Quebec city is public and you can walk through the streets and view the fine improvements that are going on there for the benefit of the whole country.
I have little more to say. But before concluding I would point this out: in Quebec the American people are very well treated by the provincial government. Take Noranda and Arvida for instance: when these new towns were built the Quebec legislature appointed as mayors and councillors, Americans who were not naturalized as British subjects. And at the last session of that legislature a statute

Supply-Harbours and Rivers-Quebec
was passed, in connection with the town of Racine in the Lake St. John district, enabling two Americans to be appointed as mayor and councillor, respectively-there is another member, a municipal councillor, also. These two gentlemen, one a Mr. J. Reidy Smith and the other a Mr. K. B. Bolton, are not naturalized as British subjects. I got this information from the Department of the Secretary of State. Now, according to the British North America Act aliens come under the jurisdiction of the federal government, and I wonder whether the federal government will veto such a law giving public rights to aliens, Americans, who are not naturalized as British subjects. I should like to have some information from the government on this point.
To sum up. The only reason why, in my opinion, there is an excuse for this vote is that it is expended in a semi-public way; in a few years the money will come back to the government through another channel. It will help some people to have work there for some time to come. That is the only reason and the only justification for this vote, but I ask the Minister of Public Works and the members of the cabinet not to be impressed by big corporations; they are entitled to justice, but they are not entitled to anything more than the man in the street is entitled to. I do not say that as a criticism; I say it from the bottom of my heart. I think there should be equal justice to all. I have no reason to complain in that respect about the present federal government, but the members of the cabinet should be careful and I hope they will be in the future to see there are no grounds for complaint of this kind, because in Quebec to-day there is criticism of the excessive powers given to private and foreign corporations by the local legislature.

I understand the item is to stand, so I wish to make just a slight suggestion to the minister. I am informed that trading vessels are not allowed to enter the harbour to which this vote has reference. Will the minister kindly ascertain for me whether or not that statement is correct and whether, if this vote is passed, it will not be necessary to have some arrangement with the company which will permit the free entry of trading and fishing vessels to this harbour where we are to do the dredging?

I will be glad to obtain
the information; I understand that these vessels have access to the harbour, but I will make certain.

Since my name has been
brought into this discussion I might add just
a few words. First I wish to thank my hon. friend from Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot) for his able and eloquent defence of my conduct in this house. After what he said little remains for me to add except to say that I am very sorry I did not listen to the argument of my hon. friend from Charlevoix-Saguenay (Mr, Casgrain). I am sure that if his argument were as relevant and as pointed as the observations he made with reference to myself, the house must have been convinced that this vote should not go (lirough. As I understand it, he said that because a certain vote was passed for the city which I represent, I should remain in my seat and allow all kinds of raids to be made on the public treasury.

I did not say that; I
said that when the vote for the Quebec harbour commission was under discussion, my hon. friend from Quebec West was not so much concerned with the future, because that vote was passed very much on the assurance that later on there would be revenues coming from the harbour of Quebec. In this case my hon. friend from Quebec West was discussing the same point; he said we should be concerned about what will happen to this is'nnd in the future, when it will be depopulated, and I simply made a comparison in that way. I said then that I was surprised to find the hon- gentleman so concerned today with considerations of that kind when he was not so much concerned when the other vote was passed.

I accept the explanation
made by my hon. friend in reference to his remarks concerning myself and other members of my family, although I do not know what they have to do with the future of Anticosti; as yet my brother has not been appointed chairman of the harbour board of Anticosti. However, if the minister who appointed him to the harbour board of Quebec thinks he can carry on the work at Anticosti, he may yet receive that appointment. In any case, as I understand the argument of my hon. friend it is that when we were discussing matters relating to the harbour of Quebec I did not oppose that vote, nor did I say that the harbour of Quebec was a paying proposition at present. That is quite true; I did not say anything like that but I did 6ay, and I repeat, that Quebec is a national port, and even if it never paid interest on its debentures or on the money expended there it is the duty of the parliament of Canada to see that the harbour commission of Quebec has money with which to carry on the development of that port.
3360	COMMONS
Supply-Harbours and Rivers-Quebec
On the other hand this place for which it is now sought to vote money is a private enterprise, owned by a private corporation which keeps the inhabitants there almost in a state of peonage, and which will not allow an ordinary citizen of this country to land on the island without first receiving permission. I doubt very much whether those people living on the island can get married without permission; I know they must not have firearms or powder; I know that the animals which roam the forests cannot be shot by anyone landing on the island; I know that the fish with which the rivers teem cannot be touched and that no man going there may put a line in any stream under pain of deportation. It is even worse than somewhat similar laws we have in this country. If. forsooth any of the workmen dare to insult his majesty the governor of the island, they are deported by the next boat. That is the situation as it exists there, and I do not know a similar condition anywhere else in Canada.
Are they deported without trial by jury?

They have no such thing,
and if they had the magistrates would be in the pay of the corporation. Now we are told that we should vote $500,000 for this work because the post office there pays $2,000 a year, but the hon. gentleman should know that we are paying subsidies for the air mail service to that island and also for the vessels which stop there to get the mail. If the post office even paid enough to cover these subsidies we might be satisfied, but it does not.
I want to conclude in this way: I am absolutely opposed to this vote, unless I can obtain from the minister a greater assurance than he has been able to give me so far that there is something solid in the way of settlement and development of our country to come out of this expenditure. Unless the minister can tell us that this island is not to be absolutely owned and controlled and that the inhabitants are not to be owned and operated, body and soul, by a corporation such as this, against wffiich we cannot rise to say something in this house without- receiving the expostulations of persons even within my own constituency, this vote should not pass. I will admit that as a result of what I said the other day and what I have said to-day I may have extreme difficulty in being re-elected, but in my opinion the time has come when members of this parliament and possibly members of other legislative bodies should say to the

large corporations which are endeavouring to throttle the economic, moral and social life of the people of the province of Quebec, that the time has come to stop. We will support them so long as they wish to develop the province, but when strangers and foreigners come and dictate to us what shall be our course of conduct, I think we should call a halt.

I must declare this amendment out of order because it is a tax. Bourinot, at pages 430 and 431, on the imposition of taxes, says:
As a consequence no private member is now permitted to propose a dominion tax upon the people; it must proceed from a minister of the crown, or be in some other form declared to be necessary for the public service. A motion or a bill of such a character should properly be introduced by a minister of the crown.
The question comes under standing order 60:
If any motion be made in the house for any public aid or charge upon the people, the consideration and debate thereof may not be presently entered upon, but shall be adjourned until such further day as the house thinks fit to appoint; and then it shall be referred to a committee of the whole house, before any resolution or vote of the house do pass thereupon.
May at page 511, 13th edition, says:
The principle that the sanction of the crown must be given to every grant of money drawn from the public revenue, applies equally to the taxation levied to provide that revenue.
The principle is clear. The recommendation of the crown is always signified in matters of taxation. There is no question that this amendment imposes a charge on the people.

However, I feel satisfied that your honour will rule the amendment out of order, and my only regret is that you did not rule the original bill also out of order, for in effect it amounts to the same thing. It is a tax upon the people, just as effective as though it were imposed by the Minister of Finance. It is a tax upon the users of the bridge, and all I sought to do was to get 5 per cent of the gross receipts or taxes back into the Dominion treasury in order to assist the Minister of Finance to declare another surplus in his budget next year.

speechtext: Sir EUGENE FISET (Rimouski) moved the third reading of Bill No. 93, respecting the Sun Life Assurance Company of Canada.

maintopic: SUN I.IFE ASSURANCE COMPANY OF CANADA
speechtext:
This bill is before parliament for the second time, and I presume hon. members realize its great importance. We have given it so far this year scarcely two hours' consideration. The bill in the amended form in which it came from the select standing committee on banking and commerce has not yet been printed and distributed to the house. We have passed it through the committee of the whole not knowing what we were passing. The measure was not even printed, and here we are about to give it its third reading, notwithstanding the possibility that there are some members who do not know what it contains. I suggest, sir, that this is not very good practice. There seems to be an attempt to push the bill through the house whether it is acceptable or not from the point of view of public interest.
There are some things in connection with this bill to which I wish to direct your attention, Mr. Speaker, and the attention of the house. This bill reminds me of a pirate ship; it is sailing on the high seas of finance but it is not flying the jolly roger.	If she were
flying the jolly roger at the masthead everyone would know exactly what her objective was. But she is flying the Canadian flag on the foremast, the union jack on the mainmast and on the mizzen a burgee of goodwill to the public. With these decorations she sails on to victory. No one questions the skipper as to what the port is; no one raises any objection to the course that is being steered; no one asks anything about the nature of the cargo. She is allowed to pass by unquestioned. If she were true to her real purpose and destiny she would fly the jolly roger.
The history of this bill was given very ably by the hon. member for West Elgin (Mr. Hepburn), who analysed the demands of the company, discussing the different clauses of the measure. I will not follow his course; I will present my view of the matter from a different angle. The bill provides, as I presume we all know, for an increase in capital

stock to the amount of 82,000,000. I should
like to have some reason either from the company or from the sponsor of the bill-at any rate, from some authority-for this increase in capital. I shall deal later on with the reasons given by the company itself for increasing the capital. These reasons I regard as a mere subterfuge; they do not really explain why the company seeks to increase the capital stock by $2,000,000, Let me here observe that capital in a well established insurance company is not only unnecessary but is a hindrance to the company. Every dollar of capital in an insurance company so well established as is the Sun Life Assurance Company of Canada becomes n charge on the earnings of the company. That is its only service; it is not required. No one will argue that an insurance company which is well established requires capital at all. The capital which this company now has is more than sufficient, having brought the company from small beginnings to where it now stands, one of the most successful insurance companies in Canada or even on the North American continent. I contend therefore that as the company has been brought thus far on a comparatively small amount of capital we should demand from the sponsors of the bill or from the management or the directors just why they now seek to raise the capital stock of this company by another $2,000,000.
The general tendency to-day in connection with insurance companies is not to increase, but to decrease capital stock; the tendency is towards [DOT]mutualization, capital stock not being required at all. In this connection I think it is illuminating to read an extract, taken from the Citizen of April 23, which comes from the Mutual Life Assurance Company. He says:
An interesting announcement is made by the Mutual Life Assurance Company of Canada to the effect that a special extra dividend to the amount of $700,000 is to be paid this year to its participating policyholders. From information received from the company's head office, it is learned that the percentage of dividend wall he graded according to duration of policies, those which have been longer in force receiving a large percentage of extra dividend. The scale of extra dividend commences at 10 per cent of the regular annual dividend payable in 1928 on policies one year in force, and is as high as 25 per cent for longer durations. . .
While special extra dividends have occasionally been paid by other life insurance companies elsewhere when warranted by earnings and accumulated surplus funds, this is the first occasion on which a Canadian company has adopted this method of sharing earnings with policyholders.
I submit that it would be far more in keeping with the modern practice of life insurance companies for the Sun Life Company to use its profits as the Mutual! Life Assurance Com-

Sun Life Company
pany have used their pirofits rather than, to devise new capital issues of stock as a means of absorbing the extraordinary profits made by the company. There are two ways in which the company could handle its excessive profits, other than the course it has chosen to follow. First, the company could give to the policyholders the extra profits which it is now seeking to find some way of covering up, or if it did not wish to take that course it could reduce the cost of insurance to all policyholders both present and future. I contend that .either of these suggestions would be a far better way to deal with the situation confronting the Sun Life Assurance Company at the moment that the one proposed in the bill.
Next I want, to direct attention to the amount paid by the shareholders for the $2,000,000 of stock they have under control. By examination I find that the shareholders of this company have paid in all $380,000; that is the entire amount of the capital invested in the Sun Life Assurance Company by the shareholders. They have received profits on that amount; 'they have received other profits on other amounts which they have been able to control by certain manipulations; they have voted bonuses to themselves and in that way have paid the rest of the $2,000,000. and they are charging profits on that amount, making from 25 per cent to 30 per cent annually on their investments. Not only that, 'but from 'that small initial investment of $380,000 the shareholders to-day have standing to their credit $30,000,000. Surely these earnings are sufficient .to make us pause for a moment and ask whether we will give them a further gift of $2,000,000, by means of which they will pry out of the pockets of their policyholders another enormous amount in profits, equal to the amount which they are now getting on the $2,000,000 of stock already issued.
I regard this bill as a scheme to obtain greater profits for the company, and to obtain them in such a way as to enable the company to pose as a benefactor to the public, through its magnanimity in reducing the profits from 10 per cent, to which they are entitled by law. to 5 per cent. Meanwhile the company will get twice this amount by increasing its capital stock unnecessarily. The company almost boasts that it takes a profit of only 5 per cent when it might take 10 per cent, and attempts to make a plea to parliament rather on compassionate grounds as to why this bill should go through. Let me turn to a statement which appeared in the large daily papers throughout Canada a short time ago, coming directly from the manager of this company. In its headlines this statement bears that mark
of servility which characterizes the attitude of most daily papers towards huge corporations, a servility which I sometimes wonder whether parliament has been able to escape. This article says:
The phenomenal record of the Sun Life Assurance Company is an inspiration to all Canadians. Its income of $102,000,000 is already equal to the total revenue of the government of Canada in the year 1910, and $38,000,000 is certainly an amazing sum to have earned as profit in one year. Not many corporations anywhere can report such figures. The president's intimate, practical comments at the annual meeting explaining how these huge profits were made were illuminating.
They were illuminating!
Of even greater moment, however, were his statements regarding the danger that this great Canadian institution may pass from Canadian control. Some months ago. Mr. Macaulay referred to the activity of Wall street in the buying of Sun Life stock, and cautioned policyholders and shareholders of the mpnace it involved to an institution which was founded and developed by Canadians and which lias obtained its phenomenal growth under Canadian management. Subsequent events have justified these misgivings, and at the meeting to-day the first public intimation was given that the Sun Life directors are seeking legislation at the present session of parliament which is intended to effectively forestall this danger.
This news item, which was sent to the great dailies of Canada., and which contains the announcement that a bill was to be introduced to save this great company from passing into the hands of Wall street, was advertising, carefully guided and planned in order to affect the minds of members of parliament when the bill was presented. Now let me read a very short extract from the report made by Mr. Macaulay, general manager of the company, at the last annual meeting:
The new assurances completed amounted to $328,000,000. an increase of over $62,500,000. The amount in force at the close of the year had risen to $1,487,000,000, and at the present moment is well over $1,500,000,000. The income exceeded $102,000,000. an increase over the previous year of $23,800,000. To me, this is very impressive. Not only has this item passed the one hundred million mark, but the increase alone is equal to what was our total income but eight years ago, which had been accumulated by forty-nine years of strenuous effort. A life company with a total income no greater than our increase would be an important corporation.
The assets have increased by $56,000,000, and now exceed $400,000,000. But the most wonderful of all these wonderful figures is the amount earned as profit-$38,000,000. How great this figure is may be judged from the fact that the earnings of the previous year, in which we so rejoiced, were $20,500,000.
There was an increase last year in the earnings of this company amounting to approximately $18,000,000, and the total amount which the company made last year was $38,-

I do not know whether the tendency you mention has been more marked since the amendment of your bill at the last session or not, hut I shall be glad to know if, in your opinion, a requirement that a larger proportion than a bare majority of directors be Canadians and British subjects, would have a deterring effect on the dealings in the stock. I understand that the movement of the shares to New York had commenced before the amendment of your charter respecting the board of directors last session, and I had a feeling at the time that possibly the change proposed then permitting directors other than British subjects might strengthen that tendency rather than diminish it. You will probably be able to say whether or not this is so.
You will, of course, have noticed a somewhat similar movement with reference to Canadian bank shares, which indicate that amount of japital is not a determining feature.
I am glad to know that so large a proportion of your capital is in the hands of yourself and associates and in the hands of those who may be fairly well counted on to preserve the company as a Canadian company.
In that communication it is revealed that the company itself, by altering the regulations with respect to its directors, made it possible for United States directors to come in, whereas before they could not. Therefore it would appear that they were not very much afraid of the United States at that time. Moreover, as is made clear in this letter from the Superintendent of Insurance, the amount of stock issued by any company is no guarantee of its control remaining in Canada. This is a letter from Mr. Macaulay to the Superintendent of Insurance on the subject:
I have your favour of the 23rd.
I am quite sure that the question of the nationality of directors has nothing to do with the movement in our stock. At present the buying appears to be only for investment, but if a New York group should obtain control they would find no difficulty in appointing Canadian associates or nominees.
The transfer of our stock to American ownership appears to he increasing steadily in volume. Even since I wrote you, several more blocks of fairly large amount have gone across the boundary lines. Several other blocks have been offered to us here, and, as we were unable to find purchasers for them, they too, no doubt, will be in the United States within a few days. Another block was offered to me this morning. An American broker has just written asking for a number of copies of our annual report that he may give them to persons who may become interested in our stock. Another report indicates that it is proposed to give our stock a prominent place in the holdings of some investment trusts. This very morning also we have had a call from the president of one of the National Banks of Hartford, who wished to find out as much as possible about the value of our stock, in order that he might accommodate brokers by making loans on its securities until such time as they find customers. Mr. Wood had a long interview with him and tried to discourage him but was smilingly told that we are like most inside executives, we do not know the real value of our stocks. He spoke

of buying some for himself at $1,200 per share. Even since I dictated this letter a Toronto broker tells us that he has an offer of $1,410 per share from the United States. Almost every day there are fresh developments.
So every day in every way according to Mr. Macaulay the company wias going to be snatched from him by somebody in the United States.
I want to occupy a few of the remaining minutes of my time to deal with what the policyholders have to say about this.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I move, Mr. Chairman, that
the Port Dover item be changed to read:
Repairs to piers and harbour improvements, revote $12,000, vote $50,000.
Amendment agreed to.
Will the minister explain why the full amount was not spent last year? I am not opposing the vote. I know Port Dover requires the improvements.

This amount, of which $12,000 is a revote from 1927-28, is required towards the reconstruction of the east pier which was damaged by a severe storm on December 8, 1927, and for repairs to the vertical timbers and to the stringers of the west pier. We now propose to build a new east pier instead of reconstructing the old one. The engineer reports that practically the whole superstructure of the east pier has been demolished except for a portion recently reconstructed, about 200 feet, near the outer end of the pier. At present there remains about eighteen inches of timber substructure, stone filled, above water level. All cribs have been shoved out of line and no doubt considerable damage has occurred below water level.
Is there any provision for dredging there?
No; this is just harbour work.
Is it proposed to build a new pier?
The east pier, a little further over where the channel is better.
Will there be better protection from storms?
The channel is wider, but I do not know that there is any better protection from storms; we shall be subject to storms in the same way.
Of $25,000 voted last year for dredging purposes, only $13,000 has been expended. I presume there was still more dredging to be done there.
My hon. friend is hardly correct in saying that $25,000 was voted for dredging purposes; it was voted for repairs to the pier and only $12,693 was expended. This is part of the same project.
The amendment just carried has reference to other harbour improvements. What are those other improvements?

We had to change the wording of the item owing to the fact that the location was changed.
Item as amended agreed to.
Port Stanley-harbour repairs and improvements, $16,000.
Will the minister explain this item and say what tonnage passes through the port?

I want some hon. member to move that this item be reduced by $12,000. The explanation is that the contract with A. W. Robertson, Limited, was closed out after the main estimates had been prepared, and the $12,000 will not be required.

Item agreed to.
Southampton-repairs to breakwater, $6,600.

Will the
minister explain this item?

This amount is required for the reconstruction of the east breakwater on a length of 250 feet on the inner end of the north face and on a length of 400 feet on the inner end of the south face. This work is to be done by day labour. It is hoped that the completion of the work will result in there not being more than $5,000 to expend during the following year. Unless unforeseen damage occurs we should not require to expend any large amount on repairs to these structures for at least two years. The work is required for the accommodation of the fishing fleet and for the general traffic of the harbour.
Why done by day labour?
The engineer is of the impression that he can carry it out with his own forces to better advantage than by letting the contract. *

Perhaps the committee will remember that a few weeks ago I indicated that work done by day labour, in some of these Public Works items, was limited to those who professed the Liberal faith. I read a letter that came to me from Riviere Nouvelle, Bonaventure county, in March, 1928:
We the undersigned take the privilege of writing you concerning some public work performed at our river during the summer of nineteen hundred and twenty-seven (1927).
We Conservatives asked the foreman Mr. Richard Molley for work; he refused all Conservatives one hour's work by orders of Hon. Charles Marcil. Is this a free country, or does a man have to be a Liberal to live here? Are we to be deprived our rights in the future as in the past? At the time the work was being performed last summer we wrote the hon. Minister of Public Works and got no reply. Is that justice? Do you call that kind of work public or private or party work?
If we are justified in writing you concerning this kindly reply to our request, and oblige Yours sincerely,
Hugh Watt, returned soldier.
Epiphane Talbot, returned soldier.
Peter Gignac.
Jean Abel Thiriault.
Joseph P. Laroque,
Joseph Gignac.
Godefroi Thiriault.
Remio Theriault.
Simon LoiselfMr. Elliott.)
If that sort of thing is going on in this country it is time parliament did something to assert the rights of individual Canadians and especially returned soldiers, to jobs by which they can keep themselves at least in food and clothing for themselves and their families. It is not limited to that particular constituency, as I have said, and I would like to ask the minister whether it is the settled policy of his department to instruct his engineers that the local member shall limit employment to those who support the administration, in the expenditure of public moneys.
I must say I do not recall the circumstances of this case, but I shall be very glad to look into the question of the letter not being answered.
That is the smallest part of it.

I know of no letters coming to the office which do not receive a reply just as promptly as possible. The reply may not be satisfactory, but we always try to reply. As far as the practice is concerned, I have given no special instructions with regard to this or any other place. If the work is done by day labour we expect to engage men who will give a reasonable day's work for a day's pay. I have given no instructions as to who should be employed.

For the benefit of the committee I might say that this is the practice in vogue in the constituency which I represent. A man cannot earn a dollar on public works there if he is not a supporter of the administration. I presume the minister has nothing to do with it, but the local politicians certainly act that way.

So does the local
government.

No, the government of
Nova Scotia employ many Liberals in the expenditure of public money.
No.

I can give an instance which occurred during the last election. I asked one of the road men, a man driving a team on the road and drawing $6 a day, for his vote, and he said he could not vote for me. I said, "At least you are honest, notwithstanding the fact that you are drawing $6 a day from the local government." He was not fired for that, either; he continued right on until the

Supply-Harbours and Rivers-Ontario
job was completed. However, in my constituency it is impossible for a Conservative to get a day's work on any public work being carried on.
Mr. GARDINER. With regard to this item I should like to ask the minister if it is not the practice that when an amount exceeds $4,000, contracts should be given, and the work should not be done by day labour?

No, there is no such
regulation, but I may say that in nearly every case we try to let contracts, where we can, at a price which would be equal to the cost of carrying on the work by day labour.

Is not the minister wrong
in that answer? I am not going to quarrel as to whether or not he is doing it, but if I recall correctly there is some regulation, some order in council or some statutory provision which says that any work costing over $5,000 must be done by contract, or putting it another way, where the minister thinks it is best he may do any work costing less than $5,000 by day labour.

No. I think what my
hon. friend has in mind is the letting of contracts for $5,000 and upwards by public tender. There is an express provision in the act which authorizes the department, where it is deemed advisable or in the public interest, to do the work by day labour.
No, there is no limit.

I thought the amount
was $4,000, but my hon. friend says it is $5,000; is there not a treasury board minute carrying that provision?
No, it is statutory.

Then up to $5,000 you
can do it by day labour, but anything in excess of that must be done by contracts called for by public tender?

No, there is no limit.
Take this building, for example; it was built entirely by day labour.
But that is different; parliament appointed a special non-partisan committee and so on; that was a special provision of parliament.

That is quite true, but
there is no limit under the act to the amount of work which may be done by day labour.
Is there not some provision by which you must call for public tenders if the work is to cost over a certain amount?
I did not quite catch that question.

Is there not some
provision whereby works costing over a certain amount must be carried on by contract, advertised and called for by public tender? Under that amount contracts may be called for by private letters, on account of the expense and so on.

I think what my hon.
friend refers to is that for works costing under $5,000 we can call for local tenders, but my hon. friend can take my word for it, I think, that the act provides that contracts for over $5,000 are to be by public tender. There is no restriction other than that.
That is what we say.
There is a provision that the work may be done by day labour, and that provision is not limited to the $5,000. My hon. friend will find that in the act.

But if that is so you
could skate around any statute by saying you will do a certain job by day labour.

That is the provision in
the statute.
No, there is no limitation.

Has the minister considered the necessity of deepening the western entrance to the harbour with a view to providing an entrance for larger vessels on the completion of the Welland canal? I believe the harbour board has already communicated with the minister regarding it, but I should like to know if he has considered it and what position the government or the department propose to take. It is very necessary that that entrance should be deepened in order to provide for larger vessels.
In this connection I might say that the western entrance is rocky and it will require a great deal of blasting. That kind of work cannot be done on short notice, and the arguments that I can put forward would only be the same as were offered to-day by the member for West Hamilton (Mr. Bell) regarding the Burlington entrance to Hamilton harbour. The larger vessels which will be enabled to come through the new Welland canal must necessarily get into these ports which are the largest on the lake, and this work should be done at once. If the Welland canal is to be completed in 1930 my contention is, and I believe it is the contention of the harbour board, that some work should be done each year, and I should like to know whether the minister can give some information in regard to that. I should like to know fMr. Elliott.]
also whether vote No. 144-dredging, Ontario and Quebec, $600,000-would cover any dredging in the western entrance to Toronto harbour.

The item to which my hon. friend has just referred cannot be utilized for that purpose. The amount required for that work would be considerable, and the desire is to have it completed by the time the Welland canal is finished, but I cannot say anything further than that the matter has been under consideration. Our information is that we can get depth of twenty feet in the western channel without any blasting, but if we have to go deeper than that we shall have to do some blasting, which will materially increase the cost. I cannot advise my hon. friend to be hopeful about much progress being made this year at any rate.

Item agreed to.
