Item agreed to.
Harbours and rivers-Manitoba-Gimli-reconstruction of protection work, $7,000.
Will the minister explain this item, please?

This work consists of the reconstructing of 1,200 lineal feet of protection work which was partly destroyed during 1927. Unless this work is reconstructed a portion of the lake frontage of the village will scour away rapidly. Gimli is the headquarters of the Gimli Fisheries Limited, a company carrying on a fishing business Which handles over 1,000,000 pounds of fish annually
Why should the Dominion do this work?
Why should we not do it?

As I understand it, you do not always do protection work, and you have refused in a great many cases to undertake responsibility of that kind; you say it is a matter for the municipality or for the provincial government.

Supply-Harbours and Rivers-Manitoba
This is the reconstructing of work formerly constructed by this government.
The old Northwest Territories did it all. Is it a navigable stream upon which this protection work is being done? That has been the test heretofore.
I think it is on lake Winnipeg; it is navigable.

That has generally been the test that has been imposed. On a navigable water the Dominion government, if it has control over the water, may erect protection work. As the hon. gentleman has said, they have declined to place protection works on many of the smaller streams in the western provinces.
Quite so.

Even in regard to
navigable streams the Dominion refuses to assume responsibility for bank protection work.
That is right.

In this case the minister says that it is the reconstruction of work previously undertaken by the Dominion, and I presume the minister does not know why it was originally undertaken by the Dominion; is that right?

There is a principle
behind this, and all the western provinces are affected. For instance, the Bow river is a very rapid stream and it has eaten into the bank and destroyed some of the streets in Calgary, but thus far the Dominion government has taken the attitude that it has no right to put a single dollar into this protection work. Why is Gimli selected and other places left out? The same thing applies to Edmonton, where the river has cut into the banks and they have made unsuccessful efforts to get some money from the government for protection purposes.

This is not a river; it is lake Winnipeg, Which extends for nearly three hundred miles in length and nearly eight miles in breadth. There are very extensive settlements along the east and west shores of the southern part of the lake, and there are some docks and wharves, and that sort of thing, that are very necessary. A great deal of fishing is done on the southern part of this lake. If it is necessary to have docks,
wharves and harbours for the fishing industry on either the Atlantic or the Pacific, it is just as necessary to have them on lake Winnipeg.

The hon. gentleman is
mistaken. I am not going to leave the matter as it is, although it may take a little time. No one is talking about docks or wharves. What is being referred to is a protection work to a bank that has been broken down of a river or a lake, and we certainly have not in recent years been able to get any appropriation for that purpose.

Let me give the history
of this structure. The department constructed a shore protection 2,420 feet long, starting near the public wharf. This work was carried out in 1908-09 and it has been repaired subsequently. The wharf was built in 1899-1900 at a cost of $10,660.75 and extended in 190708 and 1912-13.
Does the hon. gentleman say that this is a wharf?
A wharf.
That is a different thing altogether. This is a protection work.

This is to protect the
portion of the lake frontage in the vicinity of the wharf. Judging from the map I should think that the movement of the water controlled by this structure was originally caused to a large extent by the construction of the wharf. At any rate for some time we have been assuming liability in this connection and I take it that when the work was started it was thought we were liable for it.

Item agreed to.
Roseau river-improvements, $65,000.

What is the explanation
of this?

This amount of $65,000 is asked to be provided towards work now under contract with G. B. Wpod, Limited, of Winnipeg, Manitoba. The work consists generally of the construction of thirteen miles of dykes, 10 feet wide on top, averaging 6 feet in height, having a slope of two to one on the inside and one and one-half to one on the outside, and of a control dam across the Roseau river in the line of the east dyke.
Is it a navigable stream?
I do not think it is.

This looks like an irrigation project.
3386	COMMONS
Supply-Harbours and Rivers-Manitoba

It is not an irrigation
project. The government of Manitoba has promised to contribute one-third of the cost of the work and land to be acquired in connection therewith, up to a maximum of $50,000, which sum has been appropriated by the provincial government. District Engineer Goodspeed reports on the 21st April, 1926:
The years 1919 and 1925, produced very serious summer floods. Last year the discharge exceeded 1,000 second feet from June 8 to July 26, and the flood practically destroyed the crops of a large number of farmers of Vita, Arbakka and vicinity.
This question has been before the department since 1893, going from worse to worse since that date. Steps to avoid further flooding in the Roseau district, in the southeastern part of Manitoba, at a cost of $150,000, will be undertaken by the provincial Department of Public Works during the coming summer.

I should like a little
more information about this. It seems to me that comparisons might well be drawn from this item rather than from the other, because this item is apparently concerned with the protection of the adjacent country from flooding from freshets in the river. Might I ask the minister if the flooding conditions which necessitate the dyke are caused in any way by some federal construction work?

I do not think that is the case. The Roseau river, as my hon. friend may know, has its main source in the state of Minnesota, although two branches, Mud creek and Pine creek, rise in Canada to flow south across the international border to the main river. These branches drain about 300 square miles in Canada, while the river has a total drainage area of 1,350 square miles where it crossps the boundary and 1,525 square miles at Stuartburn. In the state of Minnesota drainage projects of considerable magnitude have been carried out. Before artificial improvements, some 300 square miles were occupied by swamps and marshes, which during wet seasons turned into shallow lakes. While some of this swamp land has been improved, much waste land still exists, and further drainage projects are under consideration. During 1913-15, eighty thousand dollars was expended in enlarging the channel for a distance of seventeen miles, beginning at a point near the Canadian border.
On the Canadian side of the border the river for some twelve or thirteen miles flows between low banks through a flat country. The cross section of this stream is small, with a minimum of about 400 square feet, and the slope in this distance averages about two feet

to the mile. With this restricted section the waters in flood season are pushed out over the low banks and cover the surrounding country, particularly to the east and northeast, where a portion of the flood water escapes to Rat river. West of the river, the land flooded, about two miles wide, is swampy and of poor quality. It has been estimated that a total of 100,000 acres is sometimes flooded. Not only does this occur at the time of spring breakup, when it probably does least damage, but frequently summer freshets occur, which destroy prospective crops and do lasting damage to cultivated areas.

Is this a reclamation
project, or is it merely for the protection of the surrounding country?

It is not a reclamation
project.

I am not objecting
to the protection being given, but I should like to know on what peculiarity of circumstances the protection is based in this instance whereas it is refused in others where the freshets do equal damage? This is rather an important point, because a good many damage claims have been made and there have been a good many requests for the control of water. I should like to know just wherein the singularity of this situation lies.

It is claimed that this is
not a provincial liability; that it has been aggravated by certain drainage works that were carried on in the state of Minnesota. Apparently the Dominion has for some time assumed liability and is contracting to do the work to which the province has contributed.

representations may have been made about Grand beach, because I have no data here in connection with it. All I have is in connection with Victoria beach, but I shall be very glad to look it uip for my hon. friend and let him know what applications, if any, we have received.

Item agreed to.
Faust-wharf, $12,000.

Where is this wharf? I
think a lot of money is being wasted on wharves that are not required, and at the same time money is refused for public buildings where you are getting a revenue. In the one instance you are looking for votes; in the other you cannot get them.
This is in the Peace River riding.
I thought so.

I suppose it could be
stricken out if anybody-

That sort of thing is
not worthy of the minister.
33S8

Supply-Harbours and Rivers
This wharf is very necessary.
Where is it?

It is on Lesser Slave
lake. The wharf is needed at the Faust United Fishermen's landing point, which is in the federal constituency of Peace River. I understand that at present there is no wharf on Lesser Slave lake, notwithstanding that there is a large fishing industry carried on there which yields a considerable revenue each year.

I suppose that is done
by the company on whose prospectus I saw the names of some members of parliament.

I could not tell my hon.
friend.

It looks like it. In the
meantime great communities have to go without public buildings that are urgently required, while this wharf on Lesser Slave lake, some few miles from the north pole-
No, no.
-some few miles from the north pole-
That is not good advertising.

It is on the Lesser Slave lake. I should think the name itself indicates sufficient for my hon. friend's purposes. Really there should be some principle in this thing. I saw the prospectus of a fishing company up there on which appear names of members of parliament. Now they are getting a wharf on Lesser Slave lake, while communities really requiring the expenditure of public money cannot get it. That is not the way public money should be expended.

I do not think my hon.
friend wants to make statements that are not justified by the facts.
No.

My information is that
there is no wharf whatever on the Lesser Slave lake, where there is a tremendous fishing industry, yielding a yearly revenue of from $150,000 to $200,000, without mentioning other traffic, tourist and otherwise.

Revenue to whom?
Mr, ELLIOTT:	To the fishermen, I presume.
Exactly.

That is to whom it usually goes. My information is that fishing boats of

a reasonable size as well as other boats ply these waters. They have to be anchored one-quarter of a mile out on account of lack of landing facilities, and the fish have to be hauled twice, and sometimes during heavy weather it is very dangerous.

I am glad the minister
has been good enough to give us the information, but it does not detract from the statements I have made, nor in any way indicate that they were not accurate. The fishing is mostly done in the winter, through the ice, and this year an application was made to extend the time. I do not know of much fishing being done there in the summer, because they have not refrigerators to take care of the fish. I presume the next application will be for a cold storage plant subsidized by this government for taking care of the fish caught in Lesser Slave lake in the summer. The minister says the wharf will be used for tourists-tourists on the Lesser Slave lake!

Most of the fishing in
Lesser Slave lake is done during the summer. About 600.000 pounds are taken out of the lake annually, most of which goes to Chicago.

If, as my hon. friend
says, the fishing is done in the summer time, then I am entirely in error; but certainly during the past winter I had a telegram asking for an extension of the season for winter fishing on these lakes, and I know the member for East Calgary (Mr. Adshead) received a similar telegram. The department was asked to extend the time.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I understood from my hon.
friend on one occasion that there was no winter in that part of the country; it was all summer.

My hon. friend has not
got it quite right: It is always summer there in the winter.
And always winter in the spring.

take it, was prepared at the time when the constituency was represented in this house by Mr. Cross, because it has been on the records of the Public Works department for three, if not four years, and nothing has been done. with speculations, with which perhaps he is more familiar than I am.

methods in certain sections of the province mentioned by my hon. friend, but having spent only a fraction of the time that he has spent there, I am not nearly so familiar with those methods. It should not be necessary for me to assure him that everything is put into these estimates with the utmost good faith and with a view to serve the country as this government always strives to serve it.

I am happy to say that the province in which I live has been singularly free from electoral troubles; but in two sections of the west, in Prince Albert and northern Alberta, they learned a lesson from the voyage of the Minnie M. and machines that my hon. friend had more to do with as a member of the local legislature, that is, they copied certain devices for conducting elections without reference to the electorate. In one instance this was done with dire results, because it deprived the hon. gentleman who now sits for Athabaska (Mr. Kellner) of one term in this house, and in the other case the former Attorney General, who now adorns the Supreme Court of Canada, with the aid of the present chief justice of Saskatchewan, gave back to another candidate his stolen seat.

I may say to my hon.
friend that I am not so familiar with the lady to whom he refers as he appears to be. I never had the pleasure of her acquaintance.
She was one of the seven sisters.
Did you know them all?
I think the hon. leader of the opposition ought also to advertise the two other western provinces as they were during the regime of his friends.

Item agreed to.
Harbours and rivers generally-Saskatchewan and Alberta - repairs and improvements, $10,000.

I wish to supplement
something that was said by the hon. member for West Calgary (Mr. Bennett). He said that the particular part of the Bow river to which he referred was encroaching upon the streets of Calgary. It has done more than that. The Dominion government, I understand, own the boulevard facing the river, and it has been washed away in certain sections. Not only that, but the property alongside is becoming eroded. If it is justifiable to protect the banks of other rivers, I would suggest that a few thousand dollars be spent to put in piling for, say, a quarter of a mile, to confine the river to its proper channel, and so prevent further erosion.

The protection work at
Prince Albert is on the river, I take it?
On the North Saskatchewan river. It is reconstruction work. The original work was built in 1912 and 1916 at a cost of 161,885.

What is the character
of the work?

Rebuilding with pile work and filling a portion 400 feet long of protection work on the North Saskatchewan river on the waterfront of Prince Albert. District engineer Goodspeed in his estimates for 192829 says:
Some years ago the Dominion government built a pile breastwork or breakwater along the south bank of the Saskatchewan river in the central part of this city. It has stood well, but when the river broke up last spring the ice floes made two considerable breaches in the work. The breastwork is still a real protection to the bank as a whole, but with the two breaehes_ which are now made, next spring's flow of ice might destroy the greater part of the work.

Does the minister think that $10,000 is sufficient for repairs and improvements generally to the harbours and rivers of Saskatchewan and Alberta? I suggest that he include a little more in the supplementary estimates. I desire to mention some work that is being done in High River. I think the minister's engineer has looked over it. It is similar to the work done in Manitoba for
Supply-Harbours and Rivers

protection of towns from floods. The provincial government has given considerable thought to the work, and I think the Dominion government has contributed to it in part. Will the minister continue the policy of contribution? The work I refer to is for the protection of the town from flood. A few years ago the main street was flooded to a depth of three or four feet for days at a time. This is a great hardship, and the cost of constructing the necessary works would be more than such a small municipality could bear. I hope the government will do as they did several years ago-contribute to the cost of this work.

I think the Interior department and this department are co-operating with the town along the line suggested by my hon. friend. The amount for this item last year was a little over $4,000. We think $10,000 will be adequate to meet this year's requirements.

Item agreed to.
Harbours and rivers-British Columbia- Arrowhead, improvements, $1,100.
Mr. MoQUARRIE: Will the minister explain this item?

The proposed work is to discourage the meandering easterly branch of the Columbia, over the Arrowhead delta, from breaking through and filling up the steamer berth at the Canadian Pacific Arrowhead wharf. It is proposed to build a fence retard across the false channel with a view to inducing the river itself to build up a sand and silt dam and the Sand bars back of it. The retard consists of six-foot stakes driven in the ground at one-foot centres.

Item agreed to.
Crooked. Pack and Parsnip rivers, improvements, $3,500.
What is the extent of the work to be done on these rivers?

This work is to facilitate and make less arduous and dangerous the navigation of this waterway for trappers, traders and others' going into the upper Peace River country to investigate the possibilities there. The known freight passing down the river in 1925-26 was 100 tons of general freight, supplies and so forth, but the actual amount was probably considerably more. The catch of furs coming out would fall within 20 per cent, either way, of $60,000. The traffic is by open boats, usually with outboard motors attached.

Item agreed to.

Fraser river: in full and final settlement of claim o-f N. E. Broley, in connection with contract for dam at Woodward's slough, $11,639.74.
Explain.

This is required in full settlement of the diaim of N. E. Broley in connection with a contract for a darn at Woodward's slough. In a memorandum of December 13 the chief engineer recommends the following amounts to be paid: on Broley's claim, $7,038.77; on subcontractor's claim, $4,600.
What is the nature of the trouble?
The department made a change in the dasign of work, occasioning a loss to Mr. Broley. We find he sustained a loss of $8,226 due to outlay on construction over and above the amount of the estimate.

Item agreed to.
Fraser river, improvements, $150,000.
Mr. MoQUARRIE: What does this include?

This amount is asked for improvements on the Fraser river as follows:
(1)	Sapperton bar-construction of dyke No. 1, $25,000.
(2)	Steveston-repairs and extension of Woodward's training wall, $25,000.
. (3) Steveston-towards extension of north jetty, approximately 5,000 feet, $100,000.
Is any dredging done there?

No, not in this item.
Mr. MoQUARRIE: These works, I understand, have all been recommended by the resident engineer, and I have no doubt they are necessary. The work being done on the Fraser river is justified. The shipping to the port has very largely increased, as the minister knows, and New Westminster is becoming one of the important ports on the Pacific. Will the minister inform the committee what is the minimum depth of the channel at present and what objective the department is striving for in connection with the channel from New Westminster to the gulf? As the minister no doubt knows, the draught of vessels coming into the ports of the Pacific has very materially increased of late years. The Minister is also aware that there are certain ships which so far have not been able to get into New Westminster for business there. I understand that the objective of the department is and has been to provide a sufficient depth to enable ships which would naturally do business in this port to get in there so as to take out the products, which

Supply-Harbours and Rivers
are being manufactured in New Westminster and on the Fraser river, to the markets of the world. I do not wish to take up the time of the committee unnecessarily, but I desire some information on this matter.
We have been able to get a minimum depth of twenty-seven feet, which is sufficient for present requirements. That is our information.

Does the minister suggest that twenty-seven feet is the objective? According to my information that is not sufficient for ships which want to get into the port now. The former objective of the department was a thirty-foot channel, and the demand now is for a thirty-five foot channel, which seems to be absolutely necessary. Surely the minister does not say that he considers a twenty-seven-foot channel sufficient for that port. I do not think he intended to make that Statement.

I am told that the training piers which are being constructed are expected so to guide the course of the river as to scour it out and keep the channel sufficiently clear for purposes of navigation. It is quite true that the demand is for a thirty-five-foot channel, 'but a twenty-seven-foot channel seems to meet present requirements. I do not think I should go so far as to say that it will suffice for all time, but if the training piers work out as Satisfactorily as we hope they will the depth will increase.
More than twentyseven feet?
Yes.

The question I asked
was as to the objective of the department. I know that the answer given on former occasions was that it was thirty feet, and if the minister is going to cut it down to twenty-seven feet there must be something wrong.

We are at twenty-seven
feet now, and it will be a matter of experience, to a large extent, as to what amount of scouring will take place and to what they will be increased. We have no doubt that they will increase.

I have been complaining time after time in this house because of the manner in which the works on the Fraser river have been carried on. I have not objected to what has been done; I do not say the department is not accomplishing anything, but I have complained about the delay in giving a sufficiently deep channel for that port, a channel demanded by the citizens
in that vicinity and the people who are doing business in the port, and which is warranted by the amount of business available. I have suggested from time to time that a contract should be let to provide a thirty-five foot channel from New Westminster to the gulf. This afternoon the minister explained quite logically that in many cases it was found advantageous to let contracts for works in his department. I am suggesting now that this is a case where a contract should be let to finish up this work, which has already taken so long. I quite understand that the engineers of the department have been working on this matter for many years, and that lately they have been devoting a great deal of attention to it; I realize the study which has been given to the subject by Mr. Cameron, the chief engineer. I think he really does take an interest in this work and that he is endeavouring to do his best. He seems to be a very capable engineer, but I am objecting to the policy of the department, the policy of delay, of waiting to see what results will be produced by the construction of certain works. All the engineers have said that there are no engineering difficulties in the way of providing a satisfactory channel from New Westminster to the gulf. There are hon. members of this house who have visited New Westminster and who have gone from there to the gulf; they know the amount of business offering; they know the advantages of the port, the details of which I am not going into at present. I am very much surprised that the minister should be content with the results so far attained, and I impress upon him the fact that the people out there are not going to be satisfied when they learn that he thinks a twenty-seven foot channel is sufficient for the needs of the port.
My hon. friend misunderstood me.

The minister did not
mean that? I do not think he really did mean what he said, but he must realize the necessity for a channel deeper than that.
Then there is another matter which I have mentioned from time to time in this house and to which no particular attention has been given; I refer to the dredge 303. That is a very old dredge which has been operating for some 25 or 30 years; it is a suction dredge, sucking up sand and water into its hold and then taking that sand and water to the gulf and discharging it. I do not know what the engineering department think about dredge 303, but certainly the opinion of the people of that district seems to be unanimous that it has outlived its usefulness, if it ever had any. There is another type of dredge which has
Supply-Harbours and Rivers

done valuable work in connection with the channel of that river; I refer to the dredge King Edward. Again I am going to suggest to the minister that some investigation should be made into that matter. I am not suggesting that the one dredge, the King Edward, will be sufficient, but I do say that the dredge 303 should be replaced by a modern, up-to-date dredge of the King Edward type. I also understand there has been some kind of investigation conducted into the matter of dredge 303 by a special investigator sent out by the department. According to my information the investigator did his work in March of this year, and I should like to know if any report has been made, the nature of that report and what action is going to be taken in regard to it.
Then there is one other matter I should like to mention, in regard to the compensation for Sunday work to be allowed the employees working on the Fraser river dredges. There is an order in council which provides that no employee of the Dominion government shall be employed on Sunday except in cases of necessity, and that in such cases compensation shall be provided. With regard to the men employed on the Fraser river dredges, no compensation has been allowed for this Sunday work. I know the matter has been before the department several times; various suggestions have been made but nothing has been done to meet the situation. I would ask the minister whether he does not think it about time that this matter was settled. If the men cannot have their Sundays off at least they should be given compensation for that extra work.

I have very pleasant recollections of a visit to British Columbia last summer and a trip over a short part of the Fraser river. I can bear witness to this fact, at any rate, that the people of New Westminster are very anxious that they should have a deeper channel to the ocean. I suggest that the minister have his engineers report to him on the cost of providing a somewhat deeper channel from New Westminster than exists at present, so that at least a large number of the vessels which call at Pacific coast ports would be able to reach New Westminster. I am interested in the question because I think it would be of advantage to the Canadian National Railways to have a terminal elevator built at Port Mann. The larger portion of the shipments would go via Vancouver, but I think a large part could be bandied at Port Mann. It would be a good idea if the minister would have an examination made as to the cost of deepening the channel.

With regard to the remark made by the member for New Westminster (Mr. McQuarrie), as to the twenty-seven foot channel, I would say that the department has a channel of twenty-seven feet, having deepened it from seventeen or eighteen feet. As I explained, that is not our objective; we have been getting it deeper all the time, and it is expected that the twenty-seven foot channel will be scoured to a greater depth through the action of the training piers. My hon. friend surely does not think that we have not had engineers examining this situation. This vote provides $25,000 for the construction of dyke No. 1, $25,000 for repairs and extension of Woodward's training wall, and $100,000 for the extension of the north jetty approximately 5,000 feet. There has already been an expenditure on the Steveston jetty of $819,642, and with what we have in contemplation, while it is not our objective, we think this district of the country is being treated very liberally. We know that expenditures must be made, as this is an important point, but I am rather surprised to hear my friend from New Westminster complain that we are not going rapidly enough. I think we have been doing very well.
With regard to the question of a day off for the men working on the dredges. They all have their Sundays off with the exception of the cook, the fireman and the watchman. These men are engaged for full time, and I do not know how we could dispense with the services of any one of them on Sundays.
We are proceeding as expeditiously as possible with the important work that is necessary at this point, and we think we are doing very well.
I understand there has been difficulty in adjusting matters so that these men would get their Sundays off.
Which men do you refer to?
The ones who are not getting their Sundays off. I am not referring to the ones who do get their Sundays off; naturally they do not complain.

They all get their Sundays off except these three.
Mr. MoQUARRIE: The men who do not
get their Sundays off should receive some compensation.

They do, in their salaries.
Mr. MoQUARRIE: I assume the minister knows the provision of order in council P.C. 1537, which contains the following provisions:

Supply-Harbours and Rivers
1.	That no employee of the Dominion government should be required to work on Sunday except in circumstances of emergency or necessity.
2.	That in the case of any such employee who by reason of emergency or necessity is required to work on Sunday, he shall be allowed, in substitution, during the next six days of such work, a compensatory period of rest of twenty-four consecutive hours.
3.	That no exceptions to the foregoing principle shall be allowed except by departmental authority, and then only in cases where there may be no substitute help available to perform the duties which are involved.
It cannot be suggested that there is no substitute help available, because there will be when the dredge is in port. I am suggesting to the minister that, in all fairness to these men, when they work on Sundays they should receive extra compensation.

I am very much surprised at the remarks of my hon. friend from New Westminster. When I hear of a salary of $2,220 for a master of a dredge, I am very much surprised that my friend's electors are not satisfied with it. In our district they would work sixteen hours a day through the week and eight hours on Sunday for that salary.
And break the sabbath?
We are not Jews in our district.
Do I understand from the minister that he will give consideration to that matter?

I shall be very glad to give consideration to anything, no matter how unreasonable it may be. I would say to my hon. friend that I do not believe there is a ship sailing or working on any water in this country on which the men have Sundays off. Does my hon. friend seriously suggest that we should have another cook, watchman and fireman on Sunday, or is the answer to his question to be: Give them more pay? These men are well paid now, and I am told that there is not a ship which does what he suggests should be done. If he can name any I shall be glad to hear him do so.
Does he do it himself?

The other men are given their Sundays off, which is very different from what is done in other parts of the country and different from the practice on board ship. On board ship the men work on Sundays as a usual thing, but on these dredges they are allowed to have that day off.

The minister, in taking the stand he does, makes it quite obvious that
there can be no blame attached to anybody else in connection with this matter. This subject has been under discussion for some time. It does not originate with me and the minister knows that.

It does not originate
entirely with me.

When the minister
makes statements like those he made a few moments ago, he is simply forgetting himself. He is getting excited. There is no necessity at all for that. That is not the way for a minister to perform. I have brought this matter up at the request of an organization in New Westminster, which has met the minister, which has met the deputy minister, which has been making representations for months about this particular matter. Then the minister asks: Do I suggest this? Do I suggest that? I am not suggesting anything. I tell the minister that these men expect that they will be treated in accordance with the law. I brought this matter to the attention of the Prime Minister some two years ago and he said that he would give instructions that the provisions of the order in council should be complied with. I think he did that.

They are being complied
with.
The intention is quite clear under that order in council that employees of the Dominion government should get Sundays off.

If the cook is gone, how
will the rest of the crew eat on Sunday?

That is very clever.
The Solicitor General is always very clever.

That is not clever; it is
only common sense.

I am quite sure he
eats enough anyway. The matter of compensation was discussed by myself with the deputy minister. There was no intimation that that was unreasonable at all. What I say to the minister now I say on the strength of representations which have been made by the Amalgamated Civil Servants' Association o>f New Westminster, who have had this matter in hand. I am not suggesting anything to him. I am conveying to him suggestions which have been by this association and by the men who are affected, and I say that in all fairness they are entitled to consideration. The minister says: Oh, yes, I am willing to consider anything, no matter



Supply-Harbours and Rivers
how unreasonable it may happen to be. I do not think that is a fair way of looking at the matter, and I do not think it is carrying out the promise which the Prime Minister made two years ago, that the provisions of the order in council should be lived up to.
There is another matter to which I referred, namely, the report of the investigating officer sent out there to inquire into the operations of dredge 303.
I did not answer my hon. friend with regard to that; I am sorry. The report has' been received and it is receiving the consideration of the chief engineer at the present time.

Is it possible to get
a copy of that report?

I fancy so, but before it
is handed out I should like to have an opportunity of having it considered by the government.

At present it is not
available?
No.

Item agreed to.
Harbours and rivers generally (British Columbia)-repairs and improvements, $65,000.

How much of last year's
vote under this heading was spent?
$58,901 to the 31st March, 1928.

I wish to justify an appeal for necessary and reasonable expenditures, not for the construction but for the repair of wharves in my district, and to do so I want to make a comparison between what the older settlers put up with and the inducements which are offered to the newcomer. Prospective settlers are invited to come to Canada and the government provides them with farms, and assistance to the extent of $7,500 for each family, this amount to be repayable in twenty-five years with interest at five per cent. For families engaging in farm work there is a free grant by way of a portion of the passage money, and that is best emphasized in the case of an ordinary family of five, say three adults and two children. To-day they can reach a Canadian point, say Winnipeg, for $67.50 as compared with 563, which was the rate for a family of the same size which came out to Canada in the earlier days. That is a saving of $495.50. I say this simply by way of preface to the remark that in my district I have one thousand miles of lake and shore

line behind which there are many communities of good, substantial British settlers who came to the Kootenay country, who purchased land for as high as $250 to $300 an acre, who paid as much more for pleating it, who planted orchards, built homes and have thereby been the means of creating very substantial communities which make substantial contributions by way of provincial taxes. The only access which these people have to the outside world is by steamer, and for that purpose they must have wharves or landing places for the shipment of their fruit and the receipt of their freight. They are not asking for new wharves.
I remember in justifying expenditures for the: citadel and Rideau Hall last year and this year the Minister of Finance said that during the war and since then very little money had been spent on those properties and that therefore repairs were necessary. Such is the case also in the Kootenay district. There has been practically no money spent in that district since the war and all we ask is the repair of those wharves by replacing the planking, by driving some new piling here and there and making them safe. I have under my hand certain items. First of all, there are in the estimates just three items totalling $4,000 for my district. I have some twenty-two items of repairs to wharves, expenditures not asked for by a member or by the settlers only, but recommended by the government's own district engineer. He has presented to the Department of Public Works a list of estimates of repairs to some twenty-two wharves at a cost averaging from $85 up. In some cases new planking is all that is necessary. Among the various items is one for $8,000, to cover the replacement of the present landing place at a settlement called Ginol. The Minister of Health, who comes from British Columbia, knows the needs of West Kootenay. He has assured the settlers that he is behind all projects for the advancement and the needs of West Kootenay. He has written to the people of Ginol, saying that an item for the repair of this wharf or landing place will be considered in the supplementary estimates. All I ask of the minister and of the government is fair and reasonable expenditure by way of repairs, knowing full well, as the government must, that these settlers have gone in, and put in the best years of their lives and all their savings. Their conditions are vastly different from the inducements that are held out to the new settlers coming into British Columbia. May I ask the Minister of Public

Works simply to give us fair and reasonable consideration in the expenditures for wharves m these places that are without needed accommodation.
Item agreed to.

There is a correction I
should like to make, Mr. Chairman, with regard to the item for Gillies Bay. The recommendation is that a float be constructed, and this is being provided for instead of the wharf repairs, and I would ask the Minister of Finance to move that the item for Gillies Bay wharf repairs, $4,000, be struck out.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I move accordingly, Mr. Chairman.

Motion agreed to.
Old Massett-wharf repairs, ?3,800.

It is five minutes to eleven, Mr. Chairman. I have already spoken on the needs of northern and central British Columbia in the matter of public works, and I wish now to take up another matter. I know that anything 1 say now will probably not avail one iota. Candidly, I do not expect that anything I have done in the matter of presenting the need for public works in my constituency, or anything I may say, will bring much reward-not to myself, but to the people concerned. But I do not wish these estimates to go through to-night without taking at least fifteen minutes to present to the house certain facts that peculiarly relate to conditions in western Canada. I feel very keenly my position as a member of the House of Commons. Having given twenty years of my life to the cause of education, believing that there is something greater than party, something greater even than personal aggrandizement; that the people's needs are above every other consideration, I trust that I shall be given the opportunity to say something which I have refrained from saying for at least the two solid years I have been here.
I am not going to condemn the government; far from it. I shall not condemn the Minister of Public W orks, but I do condemn the system we are following to-day in this young country which has the heritage of ages to look back to, and at least we should do something that will indicate no lack of concern with the building up of Canada as it ought to be built up to-day. Like other hon. members who have been here since the 18th of
Supply-Harbours and Rivers
January, I should like to get home, but there is something greater than family ties. One who represents the people is in duty bound to stand to that post to the last, and he must not forget the people in thinking of himself.
As a preamble to what I wish to say, I desire to quote a paragraph which I saw in the Ottawa Citizen to-night. I read there two little things that I thought were worth recording, written probably by the dozen of our journalists, and a man whose judgment and whose perspicuity I should think is not to be questioned. Here is what he says:
If people who sign petitions knew how little miluence they exert in parliament, they would never go to the physical exertion involved in signing them. They are placed on the table, deposited for a certain time in the vaults, and then carted away to the junk heap. Parliamentary experience is that it is quite possible to up a petition for anything, and those who indulge m it only engage in a process of industrious futility.
When I think of the petitions which I have had in my possession from British Columbia, when I think of the labour, the physical exertion, yes, even the agony these pioneers went through in the depth of winter, travelling hundreds of miles where no roads exist, to procure the signature of petitioners in order that their needs might be presented to parliament, I cannot help feeling, particularly after reading the item to which I have referred, that education is necessary even in this parliamentary assembly; because these petitions which are presented to parliament should not be treated disrespectfully, should not be regarded as trivial. They represent the heart searchings, the desires and the hopes of the people who have signed them. As it is now eleven o'clock, Mr. Chairman, I shall continue my remarks on some other occasion. Progress reported.

Pacific Cable
